title: Is it risk-on or risk-off for startups?
askedAs: are investors risk on or risk off
are markets rewarding growth or profitability
shortAnswer: Partly: investors are selective, not shut. Fund the commitments that carry proof, stage the rest behind a review date, and keep a way to stop.
directAnswer: Compare the current risk reading with the commitments you are considering. Better market conditions can support a review of expansion, but each bet still needs customer evidence, a spending limit and a way to stop.
applyHeading: Which commitments the risk reading should gate
contextHeading: Turn market changes into an operating review
context: Whether’s forecast concerns movement between operating conditions, not an exact recession date, company revenue or investment return. keyword: should startups hire engineers right now
title: Should startups hire engineers right now?
askedAs: should I hire a second engineer
grow the engineering team or hire developers
shortAnswer: Hire when a specific delivery, reliability or revenue bottleneck justifies the full cost and the downside cash plan can fund the role.
directAnswer: Name the work an additional engineer unlocks and compare hiring with reducing scope or reassigning capacity. Approve the role only with a funded ramp period and a measurable outcome; a market score cannot establish that need.
applyHeading: When one more engineer is worth hiring
contextHeading: Make the engineering hiring case
context: A reliability hire may protect existing revenue without a directly attributable payback period. A growth hire needs evidence that capacity, rather than weak demand, limits results. Use different evidence for those cases instead of applying one payback cutoff to every engineering role.
companyInputs: The delivery backlog, incident load or customer commitment this role would address.
Salary, benefits, recruiting and onboarding costs, including management capacity during ramp.
Cash remaining after the hire in a downside plan and a dated outcome review.
decisionNote: Approve [role] to address [bottleneck] within [cost envelope]. Hold further hiring if [cash or outcome limit] is breached. Reopen after [funding and delivery evidence]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

title: Should startups slow roadmap expansion?
askedAs: should we cut scope on the roadmap
shortAnswer: Cut new scope if it would push out work customers are counting on, or if you don't have the people for it. Protect work that clearly delivers or keeps customers.
directAnswer: Separate committed delivery from optional expansion. Stage new scope behind customer evidence and a capacity check, then revisit it when the cash plan and team can support the next milestone.
applyHeading: Which roadmap work to keep and which to stage
contextHeading: Prioritize the roadmap during a downturn
context: A tighter budget should change the amount of work committed, not quietly lower the reliability of work already promised. Compare initiatives by customer consequence, remaining cost and time to evidence. Market guidance informs the review; it does not rank your backlog.
companyInputs: Customer commitments, retention risks and reliability work already funded.
Remaining cost and capacity for each initiative, including maintenance after launch.
The next customer validation milestone and which work would be displaced.
decisionNote: Keep [core commitments] and defer [new scope]. Pause expansion if [capacity or cash limit] is crossed. Resume at [customer milestone] with [funded capacity]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

title: Should startups raise capital now?
askedAs: is now a good time to raise money
should we raise a seed round
should we raise a series A or wait
go out to investors and raise a round
shortAnswer: Prepare now if the time to close a round plus a delay would leave less than your minimum cash buffer. Do not wait for better conditions to start.
directAnswer: Work backward from the date cash would reach your minimum buffer. Include preparation, investor conversations, diligence and a delayed close; do not wait for better market conditions if that leaves the company unable to fund its plan.
applyHeading: When to start the raise
contextHeading: Raise now or extend runway?
context: Separate preparing a raise from accepting its terms. Compare an equity raise with a smaller operating plan using the same milestone and cash assumptions. Better public-market conditions do not establish investor demand for your round, and public SaaS multiples do not set a private valuation.
companyInputs: Downside cash runway and the minimum cash buffer you have committed to hold.
Time and cost to a fundable milestone, plus the expected fundraising process and delay allowance.
Investor conversations, acceptable dilution and terms, and a plan if the round does not close.
decisionNote: Begin [preparation or investor outreach] by [date] to fund [milestone]. Revisit the plan if [cash date or investor evidence] slips. Accept terms within [agreed limits]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

title: When should startups cut burn?
shortAnswer: Review burn when your cash plan no longer funds the next milestone with a contingency buffer; tighter funding conditions make that review more urgent.
directAnswer: Model a slower revenue or fundraising case before approving more recurring spend. Reduce commitments that do not protect delivery, retention or the next milestone, and set a cash buffer for restoring them.
audience: Founders, CFOs, fractional CFOs and operations leaders
applyHeading: Where to cut first
contextHeading: Extend runway without an automatic hiring freeze
context: Cash runway is available cash divided by monthly net burn when burn is positive and stable. Use a cash-flow forecast when collections, renewals or one-off payments vary. Compare savings after cancellation costs and lost revenue; a cut that weakens retention can leave less cash than the headline saving suggests.
companyInputs: Available cash, monthly net burn and payment dates in a downside case.
Cost and time to the next revenue or financing milestone, including a contingency buffer.
Spend that can be stopped or renegotiated, its exit costs and the delivery or retention it protects.
decisionNote: We will reduce [spend] by [amount] to fund [milestone]. Protect [delivery or retention commitment]. Restore spend when [cash buffer and business result] hold. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

title: Should we freeze hiring this week?
askedAs: is it time for a hiring freeze
should I hire now or wait
shortAnswer: Freeze hiring when your cash plan can't support new commitments, and decide on backfills and critical roles one by one.
directAnswer: Review open requisitions against cash, customer commitments and existing capacity. Give every exception a named approver, a full cost and a review date, and define the evidence needed to reopen hiring.
applyHeading: Which open roles to keep
contextHeading: Set hiring freeze and reopening criteria
context: A freeze controls new commitments; it will not resolve workload or determine which work can stop. Pair it with a scope review so the remaining team can meet the commitments you keep. Reopening should depend on affordable capacity needs as well as improving market conditions.
companyInputs: Cash impact of approved offers, open requisitions and essential backfills.
Work to stop or defer if vacancies remain unfilled.
The cash buffer, workload evidence and approver required to reopen a role.
decisionNote: Hold [requisitions] and allow exceptions for [specific need]. Defer [work] to match capacity. Reopen when [cash and workload criteria] hold. Approver: [name]. Review: [date].

keyword: should we expand sales headcount now
title: Should we expand sales headcount now?
askedAs: should we hire more sales reps
shortAnswer: Add sales capacity when qualified demand exceeds current coverage and the cash plan can fund recruiting, ramp and the sales cycle.
directAnswer: Check whether the bottleneck is sales capacity or insufficient qualified demand. Add a small cohort of reps only after the existing team demonstrates repeatable conversion and the downside plan funds their ramp.
applyHeading: When more sales hires pay off
contextHeading: Separate sales capacity from demand quality
context: Hiring more reps cannot by itself repair weak demand or poor retention. Compare performance by tenure and territory so a few productive reps cannot hide a weak ramp process. Set a company-specific payback limit against gross margin and available cash.
companyInputs: Qualified demand, win rate and coverage per fully ramped rep.
Recruiting cost, compensation, ramp duration and sales-cycle length.
Gross margin, collections and cash remaining if the new cohort ramps slowly.
decisionNote: Add [number] reps in [segment] within [cost envelope]. Pause the next cohort if [demand or ramp target] is missed. Resume after [conversion and cash evidence]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

keyword: should we delay new product lines
title: Should we delay new product lines?
askedAs: should we launch a new product
shortAnswer: Delay a new product line when demand is unproven or its build and support costs would put the core business at risk.
directAnswer: Fund the smallest test that can establish demand before committing to a full product line. Set a customer milestone, a spending limit and an exit condition, including the ongoing support the product would require.
applyHeading: How to test a new product line first
contextHeading: Compare a new product with investing in the core
context: Customer requests are a starting point, not proof of willingness to pay or sustained use. Compare the new line with the best use of the same capacity in the existing product. Keep discovery reversible until customers and the cash plan justify a larger commitment.
companyInputs: Evidence of paid demand or repeated use from the intended customer segment.
Build, launch and ongoing support costs alongside the opportunity cost to the core product.
Experiment budget, success milestone and the condition for stopping the test.
decisionNote: Test [product hypothesis] with [customer group] inside [budget]. Stop if [evidence target] is missed. Expand only after [demand proof and funded support]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

keyword: how fast should we scale go to market
title: How fast should we scale go-to-market?
askedAs: should we expand into new markets
should we spend more on ads
shortAnswer: Increase go-to-market spend in steps only when retention, conversion and gross-margin-adjusted payback support the added cash commitment.
directAnswer: Set the next spending increment against a proven customer segment or channel. Pause further increases when conversion, retention or payback misses the agreed range; resume after new cohort evidence supports the cash plan.
audience: Growth leaders, CROs and finance partners
applyHeading: How fast to add go-to-market spend
contextHeading: Connect acquisition-cost payback to available runway
context: Customer acquisition cost (CAC) payback estimates how long customer gross profit takes to recover what it cost to win the customer. A blended average can hide an expensive channel or weak cohort. Compare incremental acquisition cost, cash collection timing and retention before treating efficient past growth as evidence for a larger budget.
companyInputs: Acquisition cost and gross-margin-adjusted payback by channel and customer cohort.
Retention, conversion and cash collection timing for the customers being added.
The spending increment, test duration and cash buffer if results arrive late.
decisionNote: Increase [channel] spend by [amount] for [test period]. Pause the next increase if [conversion, retention or payback limit] is missed. Resume after [cohort evidence]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

title: How to brief executives on market conditions
askedAs: market context for a board update
macro section of an investor update
what to tell the board about the economy
shortAnswer: Brief executives on the dated change, the decision it affects, the company evidence and the trigger for revisiting it.
directAnswer: Keep the briefing to one decision note with a source date and an owner. State what changed externally, whether it changes the company plan, and the business evidence required before acting.

contextHeading: A market-conditions note for an executive meeting

For a portfolio review, use the same questions across companies but keep each company’s runway and commitments separate. Historical reconstructions provide context; published weekly briefs document what was actually recorded.

The company decision affected, its owner and the internal evidence supporting a change.
The approval requested, review date and condition that would reverse the decision.

keyword: how much runway do we need
title: How much runway should we have before we raise?
askedAs: how many months of runway do we need
how much cash do we need before fundraising
shortAnswer: Size cash to the safe band for the current conditions — 9 to 18 months of runway in Sunny conditions, 15 to 24 in Cloudy, 18 to 30 in Freezing — and open the raise while you are still above the band's floor.
directAnswer: Enter cash, monthly spend and revenue in the runway planner, compare the result to the band your current conditions imply, and set the raise window the planner gives: months 4 through 8 with comfortable coverage, 2 through 5 when coverage is thin, immediately when it is critical.
applyHeading: Compare your runway to the band
contextHeading: Why the band moves with conditions
context: The band is the runway planner's model: it widens in Freezing conditions because closes take longer and rounds are fewer, and narrows in Sunny ones because capital is easier to reach. Stage widens it further — seed adds three months, Series A adds two. The band is a planning default, not a forecast: the record shows how conditions changed after each line, not what a particular round will fetch.
companyInputs: Cash in the bank and monthly spend, net of revenue.
The months a raise consumes: preparation, partner meetings, diligence and a delayed close.
Stage: the band widens by three months for seed and two for Series A.
decisionNote: Runway today: [months]. Safe band: [min] to [max] months. Raise opens: [month]. If runway falls below [min], cut burn by [amount] by [date]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].

supportingLinks.label: The runway planner: your numbers against the band

title: What should startups do before a downturn?
askedAs: what if the economy slows down
shortAnswer: Work out now what each pause line would mean for your company. The stop points are already set, so getting ready means knowing your runway, burn and demand, not guessing when things turn.
directAnswer: Put cash, burn and demand numbers next to the pause lines for hiring, roadmap and spend, and write down for each what you would cut, defer or stop if it trips — so a change of conditions triggers a decision you already made.
applyHeading: Decide now what a tripped line means
contextHeading: Why the lines are written in advance
context: Each pause line sits six points past the line where conditions change, and each restart line four points inside it, so one noisy reading cannot reverse a decision and restart it. The margin study found the published margin measures distance from that line, not probability. What the record cannot tell you is your own demand: the company inputs below are yours to fill in.
companyInputs: Runway in months against the safe band for the current conditions.
Which commitments stop, defer or survive a pause in each area.
The approver and evidence required to execute each cut.
decisionNote: If [score] crosses [line], we will [action] in [area] within [timeframe]. Approver: [name]. Evidence to reopen: [criteria]. Review: [date].

title: Should we hire our first salesperson now?
askedAs: when to hire the first salesperson
shortAnswer: Treat the first sales hire as an expansion bet: fund it one stage at a time with the stage gates written down, and size it against the risk appetite line like every other new bet.
directAnswer: Make the hire when founder-led sales shows repeatable evidence — the same segment, the same pitch, closed deals — and the fully loaded cost is in the cash plan with a written stop condition attached.
audience: Founders, CEOs and heads of sales
applyHeading: Gate the hire like a bet
contextHeading: What the record can and cannot tell you
context: The risk appetite score says how willing markets are to fund risk and faster expansion; it does not say whether your deals convert. The hire is a bet on your own evidence, gated by the same line the other new bets use: when risk appetite falls below its pause line, new commitments stop — and a first salesperson who arrives just before that line is a bet made on the edge.
companyInputs: Closed deals from founder-led sales: count, segment and cycle length.
The fully loaded cost of the rep and the cash plan that carries it.
The stage gate in writing: the evidence that promotes the bet and the condition that stops it.
decisionNote: Hire [role] when [deal evidence] holds. If [stop condition] by [date], return to [founder-led sales]. Approver: [name]. Review: [date].

supportingLinks.label: Test the hire against this week's lines

title: Should startups raise prices now?
askedAs: is it a good time for a price increase
shortAnswer: Raise prices only where customers already see the value, and only with a clear way back. Hold the base price steady if churn risk is real or if buyers are scrutinizing spend.
directAnswer: Test a price increase on new customers or one segment first, measure churn and win rate, and keep the rollback path open. Do not raise prices across the board while buyers are cutting vendors.
applyHeading: When and how to raise prices
contextHeading: Pricing during a tighter market
context: A price increase is a bet on customer willingness to pay more while they are watching budgets. It works when the product clearly saves time or money; it backfires when buyers are cutting vendors.
companyInputs: Current churn, renewal rates and win rates by segment.
How much of the product's value is already proven in customer outcomes.
The cost and effort of rolling back a price change if it fails.
decisionNote: Raise prices for [segment] by [amount] starting [date]. Watch [churn and win rate]. Roll back if [pause line] is crossed. Hold the base price for [segment] until [milestone]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Raising prices on every customer at once, so you cannot tell which segment pushed back.
Grandfathering old customers forever, which leaves the new price untested.
Cutting support or reliability to offset churn, which makes the price look worse.

faq.question: How do we test a price increase without losing customers?
faq.answer: Start with new customers or one segment. Compare churn and win rate against the old price before you widen it.

faq.question: What should we do if churn rises after the change?
faq.answer: Roll back the increase for the segment that pushed back, and keep it where customers stayed.

faq.question: Is a price increase a substitute for cutting costs?
faq.answer: No. Pricing changes take time to land. Cut spend that cannot show a quick payback while the new price is tested.

title: Should startups do layoffs now?
askedAs: reduce headcount or do a RIF
shortAnswer: Cut roles only when the runway math forces it or when the role no longer fits the plan. Protect the people who ship and sell; avoid cuts that save little cash but cost momentum.
directAnswer: Work out how many months of runway each cut buys, then cut the roles that do not map to revenue or core delivery. Avoid blanket cuts that weaken the team without fixing the cash line.
applyHeading: When and how to reduce headcount
contextHeading: Headcount during a tighter market
context: Layoffs are a cash decision with a long shadow. They buy runway but cost trust, speed and institutional knowledge. Make them deliberate, not reactive.
companyInputs: Current runway in months and the burn target needed to extend it.
Which roles map directly to revenue or core delivery.
Severance, notice and re-hiring costs for each role.
decisionNote: Cut [roles] to extend runway to [months]. Protect [core roles]. Re-hire only when [milestone] is met and runway exceeds [months]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Cutting across teams evenly, which removes the people who ship and sell.
Announcing cuts before severance and notice are settled, which costs trust twice.
Cutting so deep that the remaining team cannot deliver the plan.

faq.question: How much runway should a layoff buy?
faq.answer: Enough to reach a milestone that changes the next raise, not just a few extra weeks.

faq.question: Should we cut before or after a fundraise?
faq.answer: Cut first if the raise is uncertain. A smaller team raises on better terms than a team that looks unaffordable.

faq.question: How do we keep the remaining team?
faq.answer: Say what changed, who is affected, and how the plan works now. Silence is what makes people leave.

keyword: should startups invest in retention or acquisition
title: Should startups invest in retention or acquisition?
askedAs: focus on retention or new customers
shortAnswer: Protect retention first when buyers are cautious. Spend on acquisition only where payback is short and the channel is proven.
directAnswer: When customers are scrutinizing spend, keeping the ones you have beats chasing new ones. Fund acquisition only where it pays back quickly and the message already lands.
applyHeading: Choosing between retention and acquisition
contextHeading: Retention vs acquisition in a tighter market
context: Growth spend is easy to justify when buyers are eager and hard to justify when they are cutting. Retention is the safer bet because it compounds and costs less than re-acquiring a lost customer.
companyInputs: Current retention and churn by segment.
Payback period and cost per acquisition by channel.
Which segments expand spend and which are at risk of leaving.
decisionNote: Fund retention work for [segment] now. Hold acquisition spend for [channel] until payback is [months]. Revisit when [milestone] is met. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Spending on acquisition while the product still leaks customers.
Cutting retention work to protect a growth number, which raises churn later.
Measuring retention only at the company level, which hides the segment that is leaving.

faq.question: How do we know retention is the better bet?
faq.answer: When churn is high or payback on acquisition is long, keeping customers costs less than replacing them.

faq.question: When is acquisition worth funding?
faq.answer: When a channel pays back quickly and the message already lands with the segment.

faq.question: Should we do both at once?
faq.answer: Only if cash allows. Otherwise fund retention first and keep acquisition to the one proven channel.

keyword: should startups raise a bridge round
title: Should startups raise a bridge round now?
askedAs: should we raise a bridge round
extension round or bridge from existing investors
do we need a bridge before the next round
shortAnswer: Raise a bridge only if it extends runway to a real milestone and the terms are survivable. Otherwise cut to default alive first.
directAnswer: A bridge buys time, not a strategy. Take one only when it reaches a milestone that changes the next raise. The terms must not trap you. Otherwise reduce burn to live on current cash.
applyHeading: When to take a bridge round
contextHeading: Bridge rounds during a tighter market
context: Bridges are common when the next priced round is out of reach. They help when they fund a milestone that improves the story; they hurt when they only delay a hard decision.
companyInputs: Runway today and the runway the bridge would create.
The milestone the bridge must fund and its cost.
Terms: discount, cap, maturity and what happens if the milestone slips.
decisionNote: Take the bridge only if it reaches [milestone] with [months] of runway. Otherwise cut burn to [target] and revisit in [weeks]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Taking a bridge that only delays a cut you will still have to make.
Accepting terms that make the next priced round harder.
Funding a milestone that does not change the story for the next raise.

faq.question: How is a bridge different from a normal round?
faq.answer: A bridge is smaller and faster, and usually uses a cap or discount instead of a full price. It buys time to reach a milestone.

faq.question: What terms should we avoid?
faq.answer: Terms that give away control or make the next round unattractive. Read the maturity and what happens if the milestone slips.

faq.question: What if we cannot raise a bridge?
faq.answer: Cut burn to live on current cash. A smaller company that survives is better than one that runs out mid-raise.

title: Should startups change compensation now?
askedAs: should we give raises this year
cut pay or offer more equity
shortAnswer: Hold base pay steady and shift toward variable or equity-heavy pay when cash is tight. Cut fixed payroll before cutting people.
directAnswer: When cash is tight, protect take-home where you can and move upside into variable pay or equity. Reduce fixed payroll through structure before you reduce headcount.
applyHeading: Adjusting compensation in a tighter market
contextHeading: Compensation during a tighter market
context: Compensation is the largest fixed cost most startups carry. Changing it is slower and more sensitive than changing tooling or vendors, so it should be deliberate and clearly explained.
companyInputs: Current cash runway and the burn target you need.
Fixed payroll as a share of monthly burn.
How competitors and peers are adjusting pay.
decisionNote: Hold base pay for [role]. Move [percent] to variable or equity for [role]. Review in [months]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Cutting base pay without explaining the trade, which pushes people to leave.
Moving too much pay into equity when the team needs cash now.
Changing pay for new hires only, which creates two tiers and resentment.

faq.question: Should we cut salaries or headcount first?
faq.answer: Cut fixed payroll through structure before cutting people. A pay change keeps the team; a layoff removes it.

faq.question: How do we explain a pay change?
faq.answer: Say what the cash position is, what changes, and when it will be reviewed. People accept a clear trade more than a surprise.

faq.question: Is equity a substitute for pay?
faq.answer: Only for people who value the upside and can wait. Do not assume everyone can.

title: Should startups expand internationally now?
shortAnswer: Expand only where demand is already proven and the cost is reversible. Hold new markets until the core is stable.
directAnswer: International expansion is a multi-quarter bet. Take it only where customers already ask for it and the cost can be unwound. Otherwise deepen the core market first.
applyHeading: When to enter a new market
contextHeading: International expansion in a tighter market
context: New markets cost more and pay back slower than deepening an existing one. In a cautious market, the bar for a new geography or segment rises.
companyInputs: Existing demand signals from the target market.
Cost to support a new market: legal, payments, support, localization.
Whether the core market still has room to grow.
decisionNote: Enter [market] only if [demand signal] holds and cost is [amount]. Otherwise deepen [core market] until [milestone]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Entering a market because a competitor did, without local demand.
Underestimating legal, payments and support costs.
Splitting the team across markets before the core is stable.

faq.question: How do we know a market is ready?
faq.answer: When customers there already ask for the product and the cost to serve them is clear.

faq.question: Should we hire locally or sell remotely first?
faq.answer: Sell remotely first to prove demand. Hire locally only after demand is repeatable.

faq.question: What if the new market stalls?
faq.answer: Keep the entry reversible. Fund one stage at a time so you can stop without dragging down the core.

title: Should startups consolidate vendors now?
askedAs: cut SaaS tools and software spend
shortAnswer: Cut tools and vendors that do not pay back within six months. Keep the ones that save time or revenue.
directAnswer: When cash is tight, every subscription and agency seat must earn its keep. Consolidate where overlap exists and pause spend that cannot show a quick payback.
applyHeading: When to consolidate vendors
contextHeading: Vendor spend in a tighter market
context: Small monthly costs pile up and linger after growth cools. A clear payback rule keeps money in the bank when the climate shifts.
companyInputs: Monthly cost of each tool, agency or vendor seat.
Which tools overlap or are unused.
Payback period for each in time saved or revenue gained.
decisionNote: Keep [tool] with [months] payback. Cut [tool] with no clear payback. Review the full stack in [weeks]. Owner: [name]. Review: [date].
watchouts: Cutting a tool the team relies on to hit a savings number.
Keeping overlapping tools because switching feels slow.
Renewing annual contracts before checking usage.

faq.question: How do we decide which tools to cut?
faq.answer: Keep what saves time or revenue within six months. Cut what is unused or overlaps another tool.

faq.question: Will cutting tools slow the team down?
faq.answer: It can if you cut the wrong ones. Check usage and ask the team before you cancel.

faq.question: How often should we review the stack?
faq.answer: Before each renewal cycle, and again when cash gets tight.
